The missing emperor was Jianwen. His grandfather had founded the Ming Dynasty.  But Jianwen inherited something else. Uncles with armies.
When he tried to take away their power, one uncle, Judy, rebelled.
Three years later, Judy reached Nanjing.  A commander who had once fought for Jianwen helped open a city gate.
Judy's men carried out a body. He had it buried as his nephew.
Judy took the throne as Yongle and wiped Yanwen's reign from the calendar.
But rumors said Jianwen had escaped, dressed as a monk.
Yongle sent an official named Hu Ying across China.  Officially, he was seeking a Taoist holy man.  Secretly, he was looking for Jianwen.
When Huying's mother died, he asked to go home. Yongle refused.
More than 20 years after the fire, Huying returned. Yongle was already in bed.  He got up, summoned the official, and listened until deep into the night.
The later history of Ming says Yongle's suspicions finally ended.  It never says what Hu Ying told him.
History remembers the victors. We remember the rest.
